findings.title: isinstance check uses the wrong Process class, so hung flusher processes are never killed
findings.body: In `_ensure_processes_alive`, `process.kill()` is now guarded by `if isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)`. The real flusher processes are created via `self.mp_context.Process` where `mp_context = multiprocessing.get_context("spawn")`, so they are instances of `multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess` — a sibling class of `multiprocessing.Process` (both subclass `BaseProcess`), and `isinstance(spawn_process, multiprocessing.Process)` is always False (the file's own type annotation on `self.processes` acknowledges the type is `SpawnProcess`). Before this change the kill was unconditional; the new guard silently disables it for every production flusher process (it only 'works' to skip threads, which was its presumed intent). Consequence: when a flusher process is detected as hung (cause="hang"), the old process is left running while `_create_process_for_shards` immediately starts a replacement handling the same shards, so two (and with repeated restarts, up to MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS) flusher processes concurrently flush the same Redis shards and keep duplicate Kafka producers alive. The check should be inverted to exclude threads instead, e.g. `if not isinstance(process, threading.Thread)`.

findings.title: join()'s terminate() is dead code for spawn flusher processes
findings.body: In `join()`, `if isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process): process.terminate()` uses the same wrong isinstance check: spawn flusher processes are `multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess` instances, never instances of `multiprocessing.Process`, so `terminate()` is never executed for real flusher processes. This pattern predates the PR but is carried into the new per-process loop: any flusher process still alive after the join deadline (the loop `break`s once the deadline passes, so later processes don't even get their wait loop) is left running and only dies via the daemon flag at interpreter exit, potentially mid-produce with unflushed Kafka futures. Additionally, `remaining_time` is computed at the top of the loop and never used other than the `<= 0` check.

findings.title: time.sleep(0.1) in test_basic is a no-op because time.sleep is monkeypatched
findings.body: The test adds `time.sleep(0.1)` with the comment "Give flusher threads time to process after drift change", but line 15 of the same test does `monkeypatch.setattr("time.sleep", lambda _: None)`, which patches the `sleep` attribute of the `time` module globally — including the call on line 62. The sleep therefore does nothing and the comment is misleading. The test only passes because `step.join()` provides the actual synchronization with the flusher thread; if a future reader relies on this sleep for timing it will be a source of flakiness confusion. Either remove the line/comment or use the real sleep (e.g. via `time.sleep` saved before patching).

findings.title: Inconsistent metric tag keys 'shard' vs 'shards' on flusher timers
findings.body: The new per-process metrics use `tags={"shard": shard_tag}` for `spans.buffer.flusher.produce` and `spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes`, but `tags={"shards": shard_tag}` for `spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce` (line 199). Since these timers describe the same per-process shard grouping, the mismatched tag key means dashboards and alerts that group or filter by `shard` will silently miss the `wait_produce` series (and vice versa for `shards`). Unify the tag key across all three metrics.
